findings.title: Google refresh stores the safeParse wrapper instead of the parsed tokens
findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the zod safeParse result ({ success, data }), not the parsed data. Here that wrapper is assigned to `key` and written to credential.key on every token refresh, regardless of whether sync is enabled. The stored key becomes { success: true, data: {...} }. On the next call, googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) in googleAuth (line 75) finds no top-level access_token/refresh_token and throws, so Google Calendar stops working for that user after the first hourly refresh. Other callers (Office365, Zoom, Salesforce) correctly read .success/.data. Return or store `.data` here.

findings.title: Sync-mode schema computes keys from z.string().toString(), dropping every field except access_token
findings.body: z.string().toString() is a constant (Object's toString, '[object Object]'), not a key pattern, so both computed keys collapse into one property and the second (z.unknown().optional()) overrides the first. The schema therefore validates only access_token. Zod strips unknown keys by default, so when sync is enabled (line 16) expires_in, expiry_date, refresh_token and other fields are removed from .data. Callers then compute with undefined: Zoom computes expiry_date = Date.now() + undefined*1000 (NaN, serialized to null, which makes zoomTokenSchema reject the stored key); Zoom and Google also persist the refresh_token placeholder; Salesforce saves a key without instance_url; Office365 keeps its old expires_in and refreshes on every call. The intended 'any numeric property is expiry' needs passthrough or a different shape.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string 'refresh_token'
findings.body: When a refresh response has no refresh_token, this writes the placeholder string 'refresh_token' into the parsed data. Callers persist that value: Office365 (CalendarService.ts line 264) spreads tokenResponse.data over the stored credential, overwriting the valid refresh token with 'refresh_token'. The next refresh then sends a bogus token and fails with invalid_grant. In sync mode the minimum schema always drops refresh_token, so every sync refresh replaces it. Leave the field undefined and keep the existing refresh token instead.

findings.title: Helper both throws on failure and returns a SafeParse result, so callers' .success checks are dead
findings.body: On schema failure this throws, yet on success it returns the safeParse wrapper. Callers that check `!parsed.success` (Zoom VideoApiAdapter around line 108, Salesforce around line 92) can never reach that branch, and the error text is generic. Office365 previously logged the provider's response on schema failure; that logging was removed in this PR, so the provider error is now lost. Pick one contract: return the parsed data or throw.

findings.title: Sync branch returns a raw fetch Response that callers do not expect, and status is never checked
findings.body: When sync is enabled the function returns the fetch Response from the self-hoster's endpoint, while the non-sync branch returns whatever refreshFunction returns. Callers are written against the latter: Google reads res?.data (line 94 of googlecalendar CalendarService), and a fetch Response has no .data, so token.access_token throws. The catch swallows that and the stale access token is used silently. zoho-bigin and zohocrm read tokenInfo.data.error / .data.expiryDate on the result and throw TypeError. Hubspot treats it as a token object. Also response.ok is not checked, so a 500 HTML page is passed on as if it were tokens, and there is no timeout, so a hung endpoint blocks every calendar or video call for that user. Normalize the sync result to the shape each caller expects and check response.ok.

findings.title: HubSpot refresh writes the sync Response object into the credential key
findings.body: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response. hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn is then undefined, so expiryDate becomes NaN (line 192), and line 198 stores the Response instance as the credential key. A Response does not carry the token fields as enumerable properties, so the stored key either becomes an empty or garbage object (losing accessToken and refreshToken) or the update fails. The catch at lines 203-205 only logs, so nothing surfaces. The HubspotToken annotation on line 177 hides the mismatch from the type checker.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes the credential id as the Cal.com userId to the sync endpoint
findings.body: refreshAccessToken receives credentialId (credential.id, the row id) and forwards it as the 3rd argument of refreshOAuthTokens, which is the userId and is sent to the self-hoster's endpoint as calcomUserId. In sync mode the endpoint is asked for tokens of user <credential row id>, which is not necessarily the credential's owner. The returned tokens are then written into this credential (lines 102-109), which can attach another user's Zoho tokens to this user's credential. Pass credential.userId, threaded through refreshAccessToken.

findings.title: Zoom refresh sends appSlug 'zoomvideo' but the Zoom app slug is 'zoom'
findings.body: Zoom credentials are created with appId 'zoom' (zoomvideo/api/callback.ts line 73), and the webhook resolves app slugs the same way. Here refreshOAuthTokens is called with 'zoomvideo', the directory name rather than the app slug. A self-hoster's sync endpoint keyed on appSlug will not recognize it or will look up the wrong app. Use 'zoom'.

findings.title: Salesforce CalendarService uses prisma without importing it
findings.body: The new refresh code calls prisma.credential.update (line 96), but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a TypeScript compile error, and at runtime constructing the client throws a ReferenceError, so every Salesforce calendar operation (contact search, event creation, availability) fails for all users. Add the import.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh checks response.statusText === 'OK' instead of response.ok
findings.body: statusText is the HTTP reason phrase. It is not defined for HTTP/2 responses and is often empty, so a successful refresh can be rejected. The thrown HttpError also reports statusText with a fixed 400 regardless of the real status, and the response body (which contains Salesforce's error_description) is never read. Check response.ok and include the status and error body in the error.

findings.title: Salesforce refreshes its token on every client construction, bypassing the sync endpoint
findings.body: getClient now posts to login.salesforce.com and writes the credential row on every CalendarService construction, even when the stored access token is still valid. Each calendar operation therefore costs an extra network round trip and a DB write, and concurrent operations each refresh and overwrite the same row. The refresh also goes directly to Salesforce with the Cal.com consumer secret and does not use refreshOAuthTokens, so with CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT set Salesforce still refreshes on its own, contrary to the sync design. Refresh only when the token is expired and route it through refreshOAuthTokens.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with !== instead of a constant-time comparison
findings.body: The shared webhook secret is checked with plain string inequality, which short-circuits at the first differing byte and leaks timing information. For an authentication check on a network endpoint, compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers (for example, hash both values first).

findings.title: Invalid payloads and undecryptable keys surface as unhandled 500s
findings.body: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse throws a ZodError on malformed input (line 31). symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse (lines 57-59) throw on a wrong key or non-JSON plaintext. None are caught, so the caller gets a 500 with a stack trace in logs instead of a 400, and a self-hoster's retry logic will treat client errors as server failures. Use safeParse and wrap decryption and parsing, returning 400.

findings.title: Concurrent deliveries can create duplicate credentials for the same user and app
findings.body: The handler does findFirst (line 62) then create (line 83) with no transaction or lock. Two deliveries for the same user and app can both see no row and both create one, unless the schema has a unique constraint on (userId, appId), which this PR does not add. Later lookups that take the first matching credential may then pick a row that is not the one just synced.

findings.title: Sync update leaves a credential flagged invalid even after fresh tokens arrive
findings.body: Refresh failure paths set invalid: true on the credential (for example googlecalendar CalendarService lines 112-118 on invalid_grant, and Webex/Zoom invalidateCredential). The update branch here only writes key (lines 73-80), so after the self-hoster pushes fresh tokens the credential stays flagged invalid and remains unusable in code paths that check the flag. Clear invalid on update.

findings.title: Documented sync response contract is narrower than what the callers read
findings.body: The comment says the endpoint should return only the access token and expiry date, but callers read more. Google reads expiry_date. Hubspot reads expiresIn. Zoom, Webex and Office365 video read expires_in, and Office365 video stores the whole response as the credential key. Lark parses a {code, data} envelope and needs refresh_token and refresh_expires_in. Following the comment gives NaN expiry, or in Office365 video expiry_date = now (line 84), which forces a sync call on every request, and loses refresh tokens. The actual contract (field names, units, envelope) should be documented, for example next to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT in .env.example (line 240, currently undocumented). The PR description also says docs are required, but none are included.

findings.title: No tests for the webhook, the sync refresh path, or the schema helper
findings.body: The PR adds a webhook that writes credentials, a refresh indirection touching about twelve integrations, and a new schema helper, and the PR description says no tests were added. Several defects above (wrapper stored as the key, stripped fields, placeholder refresh token, wrong userId, missing prisma import) would be caught by unit tests of parseRefreshTokenResponse and refreshOAuthTokens with sync on and off, and by webhook tests for auth, validation and create/update.
